ddx.step1_summary:
• Chief complaint: Feeling "under the weather" × 4 days.
• Symptoms:
  – Onset/duration: 4-day history.
  – Sore throat (initially painful to swallow, now improving).
  – Runny/stuffy nose with clear discharge, nasal congestion.
  – Dry, persistent cough starting yesterday.
  – Night sweats over the same period.
  – Intermittent headaches, generalized muscle aches, fatigue.
  – Fever only in first 1-2 days; responds to paracetamol/ibuprofen.
  – Mild exertional dyspnoea; no dyspnoea at rest, no chest pain.
  – No nausea, vomiting, rash, ear pain, visual changes, GI or urinary issues.
  – Aggravating/alleviating: OTC paracetamol/ibuprofen improve fever; rest helps.
• Past medical history: None reported. Otherwise fit and well.
• Medications/allergies: Uses paracetamol & ibuprofen PRN; no regular meds; no known drug allergies.
• Family history: Grandmother with type 2 diabetes; great-grandfather with eczema; otherwise non-contributory.
• Social history: Lives alone; accountant; mild episodic cigar smoking; social alcohol; stress at work but mood good.
• Vital signs/exam: Not provided (telehealth history only).
• Labs/imaging: None mentioned.

V: Pulmonary embolism: Could explain exertional dyspnoea and cough, but lack of risk factors or pleuritic pain makes it less likely.
I: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold): Classic progression from sore throat → rhinitis → dry cough + mild systemic symptoms.
Influenza: Acute onset systemic symptoms (myalgias, headaches, fever, cough) fit influenza picture.
COVID-19: Overlapping URI/flu symptoms, night sweats, exertional breathlessness; current epidemiology relevant.
N: Lymphoma: Night sweats and fatigue could suggest, but very acute onset makes it unlikely.
D: Sinus-origin headache/pressure from viral or bacterial sinusitis causing congestion and headache.
I2: NSAID-related gastritis or side-effects: Uses ibuprofen/paracetamol, but doesn’t explain respiratory picture.
A: Allergic rhinitis: Nasal congestion and clear rhinorrhoea, but acute systemic symptoms argue against simple allergy.
T: Upper airway irritation from smoke/exposure at work parties could worsen cough, but not primary cause.
E: Hyperthyroidism (night sweats, weight/appetite changes) but timeframe and URI features make this unlikely.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory tract infection (common cold)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Classic 3–7 day course beginning with sore throat, progressing to rhinorrhoea/nasal congestion and then a dry cough; mild fever and myalgias common.
supporting_evidence: Sequence of symptoms: sore throat → runny nose → dry cough
Low-grade fever resolving with OTC meds
opposing_evidence: Night sweats are less typical for common cold
Mild exertional breathlessness (though can occur with congestion/cough)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Flu presents with abrupt fever, cough, myalgias, headaches and fatigue; night sweats possible. Course overlaps with patient’s presentation.
supporting_evidence: Fever at onset with systemic myalgias and headaches
Rapid onset of marked fatigue and cough
opposing_evidence: Fever already subsiding after only 1–2 days (influenza fever often lasts longer)
No mention of more severe myalgias or high fever typical of flu

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: COVID-19 commonly presents with sore throat, nasal congestion, dry cough, fatigue, night sweats and exertional dyspnoea; variable fever.
supporting_evidence: Sore throat, nasal congestion, dry cough
Exposure to colleague with possible illness
opposing_evidence: Course seems relatively mild and improving quickly (COVID can, but often longer >1 week)

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Could develop after viral URI with continued congestion, headache and night sweats, but duration currently too short and no purulent discharge/facial pain reported.
supporting_evidence: Night sweats could reflect persistent infection
opposing_evidence: Discharge described as clear, no facial/tooth pain

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Severe sore throat with odynophagia is characteristic, but symptom now resolving and cough/nasal symptoms make GAS less likely.
opposing_evidence: Presence of cough and rhinorrhoea (uncommon in GAS)
Throat pain already improving; no tonsillar exudates observed
No high persistent fever or cervical lymphadenopathy described
